claim: Efa6 is widely expressed in the Drosophila nervous system at larval and adult stages.
source: We used a genomically engineered fly line in which the endogenous Efa6 gene was GFP-tagged (Efa6-GFP; Huang et al., 2009). These animals widely express Efa6::GFP throughout the CNS at larval and adult stages (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a GFP-tagged Efa6 line showing expression patterns in CNS tissue at different developmental stages, as shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Efa6 localizes throughout cell bodies and axons in young and mature primary neurons.
source: We cultured primary neurons from this fly line to analyse the subcellular distribution of Efa6. In young neurons at 6 hr in vitro (6HIV) and in mature neurons at 5 days in vitro (5DIV), Efa6 was localised throughout cell bodies and axons (Figure 1E,F,H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data from cultured primary neurons at different time points showing Efa6 localization patterns.

claim: Loss of Efa6 increases axon length at 6 hours in vitro by at least 20%.
source: In all these conditions, axon length at 6 HIV was increased compared to wild-type by at least 20% (Figure 2A,B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of axon length in multiple Efa6 loss-of-function conditions compared to wild-type controls.

claim: Over-expression of Efa6-FL::GFP causes approximately 20% reduction in axon length when expressed transgenically and approximately 50% reduction when transfected.
source: The transgenic expression caused a ~ 20% reduction in axon length, which was increased to ~50% upon transfection (likely due to higher copy numbers of the expression construct; Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative axon length measurements comparing transgenic and transfection-based expression methods.

claim: Efa6-FL::GFP over-expression increases the percentage of neurons without axons from approximately 26% to approximately 43%.
source: Furthermore, we observed an increase in the number of neurons without axons from ~26% in UAS-GFP-transfected controls to ~43% in Efa6-FL::GFP-positive neurons (Figure 3B,F',F'').
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of neurons with and without axons in control versus Efa6-FL::GFP expressing conditions.

claim: Efa6-FL::GFP expression in fibroblasts causes graded depletion of MT networks depending on protein expression levels.
source: When fibroblasts were analysed 24 hr after transfection with Efa6-FL-GFP, we found a graded depletion of MT networks depending on Efa6-FL::GFP protein levels (shown and quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and quantification showing correlation between Efa6-FL::GFP expression levels and MT network depletion in fibroblasts.

claim: At low or moderate Efa6-FL::GFP expression levels, the protein localizes along the cell circumference and membrane folds, and MTs are lost predominantly from cell fringes.
source: At low or moderate expression levels, Efa6-FL::GFP localised along the circumference and in areas of membrane folds (open arrow heads in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), and MTs tended to be lost predominantly from the cell fringes (curved arrows in Figure 3—figure supplements 2B and 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations showing subcellular localization patterns and corresponding MT loss patterns.

claim: At high Efa6-FL::GFP expression levels, the protein becomes detectable in the cytoplasm and nucleus, and prominent MT networks are lost.
source: At high expression levels, Efa6-FL::GFP became detectable in the cytoplasm and even nucleus (double-chevrons in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that membrane-association might become saturated. In these cases, prominent MT networks were gone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cytoplasmic and nuclear localization at high expression levels and corresponding complete MT network loss.

claim: In live fibroblasts, growing MTs labeled with EB3::mCherry extend to the cell fringes in controls but stop at the border of Efa6-FL::GFP-enriched zones.
source: When performing live analyses, we consistently observed that growing MTs labelled with EB3::mCherry extended to the very cell fringes of control fibroblasts (Figure 4A; Animation 1), whereas MTs in fibroblasts transfected with Efa6-FL::GFP showed a very different behaviour: hardly any MTs polymerised into areas along the rim where Efa6 was enriched but stopped at the border of the expression zone, often accompanied by Efa6-FL::GFP accumulation at at the invasion sites of MT plus ends (Figure 4B,D,E; Animation 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing differential MT polymerization behavior in control versus Efa6-expressing fibroblasts.

claim: The 18 amino acid MTED motif is the key mediator of Drosophila Efa6's MT-depleting functions.
source: In conclusion, there might be some unidentified support sequences in the N-terminus, but our results clearly pinpoint the MTED as the key mediator of Drosophila Efa6's MT-depleting functions, suggesting this function to be conserved between flies and C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by structure-function analyses showing that constructs containing the MTED cause strong MT depletion while constructs lacking it do not.

claim: Only Efa6 constructs containing the MTED cause strong axon loss in neurons and MT network depletion in fibroblasts.
source: In spite of their very similar localisation patterns, the functional impact of these constructs was clearly MTED-dependent: only constructs containing the MTED (Efa6-ΔCterm::GFP, Efa6-Nterm::GFP and Efa6-MTED::GFP) caused strong axon loss in neurons and MT network depletion in fibroblasts, whereas Efa6-NtermΔMTED::GFP caused no phenotypes in fibroblasts and very mild axon loss in neurons (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D,F,G; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D,G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional analyses of multiple Efa6 constructs with and without the MTED in both neurons and fibroblasts.

claim: Efa6-Nterm::GFP tip-tracks microtubules.
source: Accordingly, we found that Efa6-Nterm::GFP tip-tracks, and that Efa6-FL::GFP and EB3::RFP co-localise at points where MTs enter Efa6-FL::GFP-rich areas in fibroblast (Animations 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing Efa6-Nterm::GFP localization at MT plus ends.

claim: Mutation of both SxIP motifs in Efa6-Nterm does not prevent its ability to induce axon loss in neurons and MT network depletion in fibroblasts.
source: However, when replacing each of the two SxIP motifs by four alanines, we found that the resulting Efa6-Nterm∆SxIP::GFP construct induced similarly strong axon loss in neurons and MT network depletion in fibroblasts as observed with Efa6-Nterm::GFP (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,F, Figure 3—figure supplement 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional comparison of wild-type and SxIP-mutant Efa6-Nterm constructs showing similar phenotypes.

claim: The presence of a well-conserved canonical MTED is a good predictor for MT-inhibiting capabilities of Efa6 proteins.
source: Therefore, the presence of a well-conserved canonical MTED seems to be a good predictor for MT-inhibiting capabilities of Efa6 proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional analyses of Efa6 family members from different species showing that those with canonical MTEDs have strong MT-inhibiting properties while those without do not.

claim: All six fly/worm Efa6 constructs tested had strong MT-inhibiting properties in fibroblasts.
source: When transfected into fibroblasts, we found that all six fly/worm constructs had strong MT-inhibiting properties, whereas the six human constructs (PSD1-4 full length, PSD1-Nterm, PSD1-MTED-like) showed only a slight increase in MT network defects that were far from the strong MT depletion observed with the fly/worm constructs; complete depletion of MT networks was never observed with the human constructs (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional analyses of multiple Efa6 orthologs from different species in fibroblasts.

claim: Human PSD constructs showed only slight MT network defects in fibroblasts and never caused complete MT network depletion.
source: When transfected into fibroblasts, we found that all six fly/worm constructs had strong MT-inhibiting properties, whereas the six human constructs (PSD1-4 full length, PSD1-Nterm, PSD1-MTED-like) showed only a slight increase in MT network defects that were far from the strong MT depletion observed with the fly/worm constructs; complete depletion of MT networks was never observed with the human constructs (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional analyses showing differential effects of human versus fly/worm Efa6 constructs on MT networks.

claim: Purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP associates with microtubules in vitro.
source: Purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP clearly associated with MTs in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but failed to depolymerise MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro TIRF microscopy data showing Efa6-Nterm::GFP binding to microtubules.

claim: Purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP does not depolymerize microtubules in vitro.
source: Purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP clearly associated with MTs in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), but failed to depolymerise MTs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro MT depolymerization assays showing no depolymerization activity of Efa6-Nterm::GFP.

claim: Synthetic MTED peptide reduces MT polymer production in vitro by approximately 10-fold.
source: We found that the amount of MT polymer produced in control MT growth assay conditions without peptide, was approximately 10-fold reduced when synthetic MTED peptide was added, whereas a scrambled version of the peptide failed to show this effect (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative in vitro MT growth assays comparing conditions with MTED peptide, scrambled peptide, and no peptide.

claim: Scrambled MTED peptide does not reduce MT polymer production in vitro.
source: We found that the amount of MT polymer produced in control MT growth assay conditions without peptide, was approximately 10-fold reduced when synthetic MTED peptide was added, whereas a scrambled version of the peptide failed to show this effect (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro MT growth assays showing no effect of scrambled MTED peptide on MT polymerization.

claim: MTED-coated beads pull down three times more tubulin than uncoated beads.
source: We found that the MTED-coated beads pulled down three times more tubulin than the same beads uncoated, and five times more tubulin than beads coated with a scrambled version of the peptide (Figure 4F, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative pull-down assay data comparing tubulin binding to MTED-coated versus uncoated beads.

claim: MTED-coated beads pull down five times more tubulin than beads coated with scrambled MTED peptide.
source: We found that the MTED-coated beads pulled down three times more tubulin than the same beads uncoated, and five times more tubulin than beads coated with a scrambled version of the peptide (Figure 4F, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative pull-down assay data comparing tubulin binding to MTED-coated versus scrambled peptide-coated beads.

claim: The MTED directly interacts with tubulin.
source: These data indicate a direct interaction of the MTED peptide with tubulin and suggest that a scrambled version of this peptide appears to passivate the bead surface reducing non-specific interaction of tubulin.
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down assay data showing specific binding of MTED to tubulin compared to scrambled peptide controls.

claim: The MTED directly interferes with MT polymerization.
source: Taken together, the MTED exists primarily in Efa6 homologues of invertebrate species and its presence correlates with MT-inhibiting properties of these proteins. This conclusion is strongly supported by our finding that Drosophila MTED directly interferes with MT polymerisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro MT growth assays and tubulin binding assays showing direct effects of MTED on MT polymerization.

claim: Fibroblasts expressing Efa6-FL::GFP or Efa6-∆Nterm::GFP display a membrane ruffle phenotype.
source: This is further supported by the observation that fibroblasts expressing Efa6-FL::GFP or the C-terminal derivative Efa6-∆Nterm::GFP (Figure 3B), display a membrane ruffle phenotype (curved open arrows in Figure 3—figure supplements 6B,H and 7B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations of fibroblasts expressing these constructs showing membrane ruffles.

claim: Efa6-∆Nterm::GFP has no obvious effects on MT networks in fibroblasts.
source: Efa6-∆Nterm::GFP had no obvious effects on MT networks (Figure 3—figure supplement 3I), and its membrane ruffling phenotype likely reflects an evolutionarily conserved function of the Efa6 C-terminus through its Sec7, PH and/or CC domains (Derrien et al., 2002; Franco et al., 1999; Macia et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing normal MT networks in fibroblasts expressing Efa6-∆Nterm::GFP.

claim: Efa6-ΔCterm::GFP and Efa6-Nterm::GFP fail to associate with the cortex and induce MT phenotypes far stronger than Efa6-FL::GFP.
source: However, even if the C-terminus plays no active role in the MT inhibition process, it still regulates this function: the Efa6-ΔCterm::GFP and Efa6-Nterm::GFP variants which lack the C-terminus (Figure 3B), fail to associate with the cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C,D), do not cause ruffling (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C), but induce MT phenotypes far stronger than Efa6-FL::GFP does (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D,H vs B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analyses of subcellular localization and functional effects of different Efa6 constructs.

claim: Addition of CAAX domain to Efa6-Nterm::GFP changes its properties to Efa6-FL::GFP-like behaviors.
source: To assess whether lack of membrane tethering could explain this phenotypic difference, we generated the Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX variant (Figure 3B) where Efa6-Nterm::GFP is fused to the membrane-associating CAAX domain (Hancock et al., 1991); this addition of CAAX changed the properties of Efa6-Nterm::GFP back to Efa6-FL::GFP-like behaviours: the hybrid protein localised to the cortex and caused only a moderate MT phenotype in fibroblasts, the axon loss phenotype was mild (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 6B,I; 3B,E) and, also in live analyses, the CAAX construct reproduced the effect of excluding MTs from Efa6-N-term::GFP::CAAX-enriched areas, confirming that this inhibition is mediated by the N-terminus (Figure 4C–E; Animation 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative functional analyses showing that membrane-tethered Efa6-Nterm behaves similarly to full-length Efa6.

claim: Drosophila Efa6 is a cortical collapse factor that blocks MT polymerization via its N-terminal MTED, with function restricted to the cortex through C-terminal membrane association.
source: Taken together, our structure-function data clearly establish Drosophila Efa6 as a cortical collapse factor: its N-terminal MTED blocks MT polymerisation, and this function is restricted to the cortex through the Efa6 C-terminus which associates with the cell membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive structure-function analyses showing MTED-mediated MT inhibition and C-terminal membrane localization.

claim: Loss of Efa6 causes an increase in the total number of Eb1 comets in growth cones.
source: In GCs of primary neurons at 6 HIV, loss of Efa6 caused an increase in MT polymerisation events: the total number of Eb1 comets was increased as compared to wild-type controls (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Eb1 comet numbers in growth cones of Efa6 mutant versus wild-type neurons.

claim: Eb1::GFP comets in wild-type neurons tend to die down upon hitting the plasma membrane, whereas they frequently persist in Efa6 mutant neurons.
source: Eb1::GFP comets in wild-type neurons tended to die down upon hitting the plasma membrane within GCs or at the tip of their filopodia, whereas they frequently persisted in Efa6 mutant neurons, where they could occasionally even be observed to undergo curved extensions along the periphery (Animations 5–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging observations comparing Eb1 comet behavior at the membrane in wild-type versus Efa6 mutant neurons.

claim: Eb1 comet velocity is unaffected by loss of Efa6 at approximately 0.14 μm/s.
source: Comet velocity was unaffected (~0.14 μm/s), but the lifetime of Eb1::GFP comets (5.04 s ± 0.60 SEM in wild-type) was ~1.4 times longer in mutant GCs, with the dwell time of Eb1 comets at the tip of filopodia being ~3 fold increased (from 2.10 s ± 0.24 SEM in wild-type to 6.26 s± 0.40 SEM in Efa6 mutant neurons; Figure 5M)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Eb1 comet velocity in wild-type and Efa6 mutant neurons showing no significant difference.

claim: The lifetime of Eb1::GFP comets in growth cones is approximately 1.4 times longer in Efa6 mutant neurons compared to wild-type.
source: Comet velocity was unaffected (~0.14 μm/s), but the lifetime of Eb1::GFP comets (5.04 s ± 0.60 SEM in wild-type) was ~1.4 times longer in mutant GCs, with the dwell time of Eb1 comets at the tip of filopodia being ~3 fold increased (from 2.10 s ± 0.24 SEM in wild-type to 6.26 s± 0.40 SEM in Efa6 mutant neurons; Figure 5M)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of Eb1 comet lifetimes in growth cones comparing wild-type and Efa6 mutant neurons.

claim: The dwell time of Eb1 comets at filopodial tips is approximately 3-fold increased in Efa6 mutant neurons compared to wild-type.
source: Comet velocity was unaffected (~0.14 μm/s), but the lifetime of Eb1::GFP comets (5.04 s ± 0.60 SEM in wild-type) was ~1.4 times longer in mutant GCs, with the dwell time of Eb1 comets at the tip of filopodia being ~3 fold increased (from 2.10 s ± 0.24 SEM in wild-type to 6.26 s± 0.40 SEM in Efa6 mutant neurons; Figure 5M)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of Eb1 comet dwell times at filopodial tips comparing wild-type and Efa6 mutant neurons.

claim: More microtubules are found in growth cone filopodia in Efa6 mutant neurons compared to wild-type.
source: In agreement with the increased lifetime, more MTs were found in growth cone filopodia in Efa6 mutant neurons, as quantified by counting filopodia that contained EB1 comets or MTs (Figure 5J,K and arrow heads in D,E; note that the total number of filopodia per GC was in the range of 10–11 for both wild-type and Efa6; not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia containing MTs or EB1 comets in wild-type versus Efa6 mutant neurons.

claim: Transgenic expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduces the number of growth cone filopodia containing Eb1 comets or MTs.
source: Transgenically expressed Efa6-FL::GFP caused the opposite effect, that is a reduction in the number of GC filopodia containing Eb1 comets or MTs (Figure 5G–L; green columns in I-L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing reduced filopodial MTs in neurons over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP.

claim: Loss or gain of Efa6 function has no obvious effect on Eb1 comet numbers, lifetimes, velocities, and directionalities in axon shafts.
source: Next, we investigated MT dynamics in axon shafts. In contrast to GCs, MTs in the axon shaft are organised into bundles, hence kept away from the membrane. Accordingly, neither loss- nor gain-of-function had an obvious effect on Eb1 comet numbers, lifetimes, velocities and directionalities (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of multiple MT dynamic parameters in axon shafts showing no significant changes upon Efa6 manipulation.

claim: Loss of Efa6 causes a strong increase in axon shaft filopodia containing MTs.
source: However, like in GCs, there was a strong increase in filopodia along the shaft that contained MTs when Efa6 was absent, and a strong decrease when over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of shaft filopodia containing MTs in Efa6 loss-of-function conditions.

claim: Over-expression of Efa6-FL::GFP causes a strong decrease in axon shaft filopodia containing MTs.
source: However, like in GCs, there was a strong increase in filopodia along the shaft that contained MTs when Efa6 was absent, and a strong decrease when over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of shaft filopodia containing MTs in Efa6 over-expression conditions.

claim: Efa6 primarily inhibits explorative MTs that leave the axon bundle in either growth cones or axon shafts and polymerize towards the cell membrane or into filopodia.
source: Taken together, our data are consistent with a model in which Efa6 primarily inhibits explorative MTs that leave the axon bundle in either GCs or axon shafts and polymerise towards the cell membrane or into filopodia.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive data showing Efa6 effects on MTs specifically in growth cones and filopodia but not in axon shaft bundles.

claim: Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons show almost double the number of collateral branches compared to wild-type neurons at 5 days in vitro.
source: We found that Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons showed almost double the number of collateral branches as observed in wild-type neurons, whereas expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduced branching by 21% (Figure 7A–C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in mature cultured neurons comparing Efa6 mutant to wild-type.

claim: Expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduces axonal branching by 21% in cultured neurons at 5 days in vitro.
source: We found that Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons showed almost double the number of collateral branches as observed in wild-type neurons, whereas expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduced branching by 21% (Figure 7A–C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in mature cultured neurons over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP.

claim: Expression of Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX causes a similar degree of branch reduction as Efa6-FL::GFP.
source: This reduction is mediated by the Efa6 N-terminus, since expression of Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX caused a similar degree in branch reduction (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of branching phenotypes between Efa6-FL::GFP and Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX expressing neurons.

claim: Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons causes a 29% increase in branch numbers in young brains and 38% increase in old brains.
source: We found that Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons caused a significant increase in branch numbers by 29% in young and by 38% in old brains, whereas over-expression of Efa6::GFP strongly decreased branch numbers by 33% in young and 28% in old brains, respectively (Figure 7L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in dorsal cluster neurons in vivo at different ages with Efa6 knock-down.

claim: Over-expression of Efa6::GFP in dorsal cluster neurons decreases branch numbers by 33% in young brains and 28% in old brains.
source: We found that Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons caused a significant increase in branch numbers by 29% in young and by 38% in old brains, whereas over-expression of Efa6::GFP strongly decreased branch numbers by 33% in young and 28% in old brains, respectively (Figure 7L).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in dorsal cluster neurons in vivo at different ages with Efa6 over-expression.

claim: Only 57% of young brains expressing Efa6-FL::GFP in dorsal cluster neurons had axons in the medulla region, compared to 88% in controls.
source: In these experiments, Efa6-FL::GFP expression had an intriguing further effect: Only 57% of young brains had any axons in the medulla region, compared to 88% in controls, whereas the axons were eventually present in the older Efa6-FL::GFP expressing fly brains (Figure 7H,K,M, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon presence in medulla regions of young brains with Efa6-FL::GFP expression.

claim: Efa6 acts as a negative regulator of axonal branching mediated through its N-terminus.
source: Taken together, our data indicate a physiologically relevant role for Efa6 as negative regulator of axonal branching, mediated through its N-terminus, most likely via its function as cortical collapse factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive data from cultured neurons and in vivo experiments showing branching phenotypes upon Efa6 manipulation.

claim: Efa6-depleted neurons display axons with swellings where MTs lose their bundled conformation and are arranged into intertwined, criss-crossing curls.
source: Apart from changes in growth and branching, we noticed that a significant amount of Efa6-depleted neurons displayed axons with swellings where MTs lost their bundled conformation and were arranged into intertwined, criss-crossing curls instead (arrowheads in Figure 8D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations of MT organization in axons of Efa6-depleted neurons.

claim: MT disorganization in Efa6 mutant neurons shows a mild 1.3-fold increase at 6 hours in vitro, worsening to 2.3-fold at 5 days and approximately 4-fold at 10 days.
source: MDI measurements in Efa6 mutant neurons revealed a mild 1.3 fold increase in MT disorganisation in young neurons which gradually worsened to 2.3 fold at 5 DIV and ~4 fold at 10 DIV (Figure 8A–F,I; all normalised to controls).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements at multiple time points showing progressive worsening of MT disorganization.

claim: Pre-culture strategy to remove maternal Efa6 still results in low MT disorganization in young neurons with gradual increase over subsequent days.
source: To assess the latter possibility, we used a pre-culture strategy to remove potential maternal Efa6 (see Materials and methods for details; Prokop et al., 2012; Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2010). When plating neurons after 5 days of pre-culture, we still found a low amount of MT disorganisation in young neurons and a subsequent gradual increase to severe phenotypes over the following days (Figure 8J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using pre-culture to eliminate maternal contribution, showing persistent MT disorganization phenotype.

claim: Efa6 is required during later maintenance stages to prevent MT disorganization, as shown by conditional knock-down experiments.
source: After this period, cells were grown for another four days under knock-down conditions (27°C), and then fixed on day seven. At this point, MT disorganisation in the elav/Efa6IR/Gal80ts neurons was significantly increased over control neurons (Figure 8K), indicating that Efa6 is not only required during development but also during later maintenance to prevent MT disorganisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments showing that Efa6 knock-down in mature neurons causes MT disorganization.

claim: Expression of Efa6-FL::GFP or Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX shows a tendency to reduce MT disorganization below baseline levels in control cells.
source: In contrast to increased MT disorganisation upon functional loss of Efa6, expression of Efa6-FL::GFP or Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX showed a tendency to reduce MT disorganisation even below the baseline levels measured in control cells (cultured in parallel without the expression construct; Figure 8I), suggesting that also this role of Efa6 is likely due to the cortical collapse function of Efa6 (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements in neurons over-expressing Efa6 constructs.

claim: Efa6 knock-down in lamina neurons causes a doubling in the occurrence of axonal swellings with disorganized MTs in aged flies.
source: When analysing aged flies at 26–27 days, we found that Efa6 knock-down caused a doubling in the occurrence of axonal swellings with disorganised axonal MTs: the average of total swellings per column section was increased from 0.3 in controls to 0.65 swellings upon Efa6 knock-down; about a third of these contained disorganised MTs (GMR-tub-Efa6IR: 0.23 per column section; GMR-tub: 0.13; Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axonal swellings and MT disorganization in aged fly brains with Efa6 knock-down.

claim: Efa6 provides a quality control mechanism that prevents MT disorganization by inhibiting only MTs that have escaped axonal bundles.
source: We propose therefore that Efa6 provides a quality control mechanism that prevents MT disorganisation by inhibiting only MTs that have escaped axonal bundles. This model would also be consistent with the slow onset and gradual increase of MT disorganisation we observed upon Efa6 deficiency (Figure 8I,J).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model supported by the gradual onset of MT disorganization phenotypes and the specific effects on off-track MTs.

claim: Both shot3 and Efa6GX6[w-] single-mutant conditions show a strong enhancement of filopodial MTs, which is substantially further increased in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double-mutant neurons.
source: To study potential mutual enhancement of Efa6 and shot mutant phenotypes, we first determined numbers of MTs in axonal shaft filopodia: both single-mutant conditions showed a strong enhancement of filopodial MTs (blue vs. orange bars in Figure 6F,G); this phenotype was substantially further increased in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double-mutant neurons (orange/blue bars in Figure 6F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of filopodial MTs in single and double mutant conditions showing additive effects.

claim: Transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP significantly improves the shot3 mutant phenotype of filopodial MTs.
source: Vice versa, when transfecting Efa6-FL-GFP to boost the hypothesised 'cleaning-up' function, the shot3 mutant phenotype was significantly improved (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing reduced filopodial MTs in shot3 mutant neurons upon Efa6-FL-GFP expression.

claim: At 6 hours in vitro, shot3 mutant neurons display a 2.4-fold increase in MDI, Efa6GX6[w-] mutant neurons a 1.55-fold increase, and shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double mutant neurons a 6.16-fold increase.
source: At 6 HIV, shot3 mutant neurons displayed a 2.4-fold, and Efa6GX6[w-] mutant neurons a 1.55-fold increase in MDI (normalised to wild-type); this value was dramatically increased to 6.16 fold in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double mutant neurons (Figure 8M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements in single and double mutant conditions showing synergistic effects.

claim: Transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP into shot3 mutant neurons alleviates the MDI phenotype.
source: This conclusion was further confirmed by our finding that transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP into shot3 mutant neurons could alleviate the MDI phenotype (Figure 8N).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements showing rescue of shot3 phenotype by Efa6-FL-GFP expression.

claim: MT disorganization phenotypes of Efa6-RNAi and shot3/+ heterozygous mutant neurons are enhanced when both genetic manipulations are combined.
source: Since complete loss of Shot is an embryonically lethal condition, we first tested in culture whether the lack of just one copy of shot has an enhancing effect on Efa6 deficiency. We found that MT disorganisation phenotypes of Efa6-RNAi (blue bar in Figure 8L) and of shot3/+ heterozygous mutant neurons (orange bar) at 6 HIV were clearly enhanced when both genetic manipulations were combined (orange/blue bar).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements showing enhanced phenotypes in combined Efa6 and shot heterozygous conditions.

claim: Cell-autonomous knock-down of Efa6 in a shot3/+ heterozygous mutant background further enhances MT disorganization in the optic lobe compared to Efa6 knock-down alone.
source: When testing the same genetic constellations in our optic lobe model, we found that the originally observed increase in MT disorganisation caused by cell-autonomous knock-down of Efa6 (black arrows and blue bar in Figure 9B,E) was also further enhanced when the same experiment was carried out in a shot3/+ heterozygous mutant background (black arrows and orange/blue bar in Figure 9C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo quantitative analysis of MT disorganization in optic lobe showing genetic interaction between Efa6 and shot.

claim: Shot and Efa6 regulate axonal MTs through independent and complementary pathways.
source: These findings support our conclusion that there is a correlation between off-track MTs and MT disorganisation. Furthermore, they are consistent with a scenario where both Shot and Efa6 regulate axonal MTs but through independent and complementary pathways: Efa6 inhibits MTs at the cortex (with peripheral MTs persisting for longer if Efa6 is absent), whereas Shot actively maintains MTs in bundles (with more MTs going off-track if Shot is absent) - and both these functions complement each other during MT bundle maintenance and enhance each other's mutant phenotypes in double-mutant conditions (see further details in the Discussion).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model supported by genetic interaction data showing additive and synergistic effects of shot and Efa6 mutations.

claim: Cortical collapse factors are important microtubule regulators relevant for axon morphology.
source: Cortical collapse factors are important microtubule regulators relevant for axon morphology
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: C. elegans Efa6 negatively impacts on developmental and regenerative axon growth.
source: the ARF activator Efa6 (exchange factor for ARF6) in C. elegans negatively impacts on developmental and regenerative axon growth (Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011; O'Rourke et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mammalian KIF21A affects axon growth and links to congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles.
source: the mammalian type four kinesin KIF21A also affects axon growth and links to the neurodevelopmental eye movement disorder 'congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles' (OMIM reference #135700; Heidary et al., 2008; Tiab et al., 2004; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and clinical database references.

claim: Growth cones are amoeboid tip structures through which axons extend during development or regeneration.
source: GCs are the amoeboid tip structures through which axons extend to wire the nervous system during development or regeneration.
evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about growth cone structure and function.

claim: Explorative MTs in growth cones can trigger extension of the entire MT bundle, thus elongating the axon.
source: The axonal MT bundles terminate in the centre of GCs; from here, single MTs splay into the actin-rich periphery of GCs. These explorative MTs can trigger extension of the entire MT bundle into their direction, thus elongating the axon (Dent et al., 2011; Lowery and Vactor, 2009; Prokop et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing growth cone mechanisms.

claim: Collateral branching of axons depends on explorative MTs that leave parallel axonal bundles and polymerize towards the periphery.
source: for example, collateral branching of axons along their shafts has been described to depend on explorative MTs that leave the parallel axonal bundles and polymerise towards the periphery (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Lewis et al., 2013; Tymanskyj et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on axon branching mechanisms.

claim: The model of 'local axon homeostasis' states that the force-enriched environment in axons biases MTs to buckle or project out of the bundle to seed pathological areas of MT disorganization.
source: the model of 'local axon homeostasis' states that the force-enriched environment in axons biases MTs to buckle or project out of the bundle to seed pathological areas of MT disorganisation (Hahn et al., 2019; Prokop, 2016).
evidence: The claim describes a published theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Spectraplakins serve as spacers that keep polymerizing MTs away from the cortex by linking MT tips to the axonal surface and guiding them into parallel bundles.
source: For example, spectraplakins serve as spacers that keep polymerising MTs away from the cortex by linking the tips of extending MTs to the axonal surface and guiding them into parallel bundles (Alves-Silva et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on spectraplakin function.

claim: Deficiency of spectraplakins causes severe MT disorganization and is linked to human HSAN6.
source: Their deficiency in any organism causes severe MT disorganisation, potentially explaining human dystonin-linked HSAN6 ('type six hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy''; OMIM ID: 614653; Voelzmann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work and clinical database reference.

claim: Drosophila neurons are a well-established, powerful model for studying roles of MT regulators.
source: Here, we make use of Drosophila neurons as a well-established, powerful model for studying roles of MT regulators (He and Roblodowski, 2016; Nye et al., 2014; Prokop et al., 2013; Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature establishing Drosophila as a model system.

claim: Drosophila Efa6 can inhibit MTs directly without interacting molecules via an N-terminal 18 amino acid motif (MTED) that binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule growth in vitro and cells.
source: First, we show that Drosophila Efa6 can inhibit MTs directly without interacting molecules via an N-terminal 18 amino acid motif (MT elimination domain/MTED) that binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule growth in vitro and cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assays, MT growth assays, and cellular experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: N-terminal MTED-containing fragments in the cytoplasm abolish entire microtubule networks of mouse fibroblasts and whole axons of fly neurons.
source: If N-terminal MTED-containing fragments are in the cytoplasm they abolish entire microtubule networks of mouse fibroblasts and whole axons of fly neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of cytoplasmic MTED-containing constructs on MT networks.

claim: Full-length Efa6 is membrane-attached and primarily blocks MTs in the periphery of fibroblasts and explorative MTs that have left axonal bundles in neurons.
source: Full-length Efa6 is membrane-attached, hence primarily blocks MTs in the periphery of fibroblasts, and explorative MTs that have left axonal bundles in neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by localization studies and functional analyses showing membrane association and selective MT inhibition.

claim: Loss of Efa6 causes an increase of explorative MTs in growth cones that enhance axon growth and in axon shafts that cause excessive branching and atrophy through perturbations of MT bundles.
source: Accordingly, loss of Efa6 causes an increase of explorative MTs: in growth cones they enhance axon growth, in axon shafts they cause excessive branching, as well as atrophy through perturbations of MT bundles.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive experimental data on axon growth, branching, and MT organization in Efa6 loss-of-function conditions.

claim: Efa6 over-expression causes phenotypes opposite to loss of function.
source: Efa6 over-expression causes the opposite phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced axon growth, reduced branching, and reduced MT disorganization upon Efa6 over-expression.

claim: The MTED delivers a promising tool that can be used to inhibit MTs in a compartmentalized fashion when fused to specifically localizing protein domains.
source: Furthermore, the MTED delivers a promising tool that can be used to inhibit MTs in a compartmentalised fashion when fusing it to specifically localising protein domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with CAAX-tagged constructs showing that MTED function can be spatially controlled through localization domains.

claim: Axons are 0.1–15 µm in diameter but can be up to a meter long in humans.
source: They are only 0.1–15 µm in diameter (Hoffman, 1995), but can be up to a meter long in humans (Debanne et al., 2011; Prokop, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on axon dimensions.

claim: Humans gradually lose about 40% of axons towards old age.
source: It is not surprising that we gradually lose about 40% of our axons towards old age (Calkins, 2013; Marner et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on age-related axon loss.

claim: Axon decay is a prominent neurodegenerative phenomenon.
source: and that axon decay is a prominent neurodegenerative phenomenon (Adalbert and Coleman, 2013; Fang and Bonini, 2012; Medana and Esiri, 2003; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on neurodegeneration.

claim: Parallel bundles of microtubules running along the axon shaft provide structural support, highways for cargo transport, and a source of MTs for morphogenetic changes.
source: Essential for axon biology are the parallel bundles of microtubules (MTs) running all along the axon shaft; these bundles provide (1) structural support, (2) highways for life-sustaining cargo transport, and (3) a source of MTs that can leave these bundles to drive morphogenetic changes.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about MT bundle functions in axons.

claim: MTs essentially drive processes of axon growth, branching and maintenance through their organization in parallel bundles.
source: Through being organised in this way, MTs essentially drive processes of axon growth, branching and maintenance (Conde and Cáceres, 2009; Dent et al., 2011; Prokop, 2013; Voelzmann et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on MT functions in axons.
